Crossed Lines of Constant Width

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Three straight lines and one moving point draw a rounded curve; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the four dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys, to move the lines and the point. Press Play to watch the point swing around the corners, and use the controls to change what you see.

Drag A, B, C or P. A dot also moves with the arrow keys; hold Shift for bigger steps.

Look for the math

Three lines meeting in three corners can draw a curved shape, not a polygon. Swing a point from one line to the next and, after six swings, it lands back where it began. Where the lines are set just right, that closed curve has the same width in every direction — even though it is not a circle.

Six swings and a closed curve

Put the three corners at A, B and C, and let P sit on the line BC. Swing P about B through the angle that turns the line BC onto BA: the new point Q sits on BA, the same distance from B. Swing Q about A onto AC, then about C onto CB, then round B, A and C once more (rotation). The sixth swing returns exactly to P. The logic test checked that gap at more than fifty thousand settings of a triangle and its point: it was never more than 10-8 board units. This confirms the page’s claim that after six rotations the curve closes in.

Six different radii

Each swing is a piece of a circle, so the boundary is six circular arcs. Their radii are the distances from each swing’s centre to the moving point. With three lines and the point off to one side, all six can be different — the page says the number “may be six”, and the starting picture here has six distinct radii. The test also checked that six is the most you can get with three lines, and that symmetric positions give fewer.

Width, and the catch

Measure a shape between two parallel lines, then turn the lines: the distance is its width in that direction. Across the whole grid of non-degenerate settings, every convex curve had the same width to within 10-8, and every non-convex one had a width that changed by more than 10-4. So the page’s “constant width” claim holds for the convex cases, exactly as it warns: move P between B and C and the curve bends inward, and the width is no longer constant. The applet gives no warning about this; this page says so in the status line.

Small differences from the applet: the Play button swings a tracer along the six arcs so the four controls stay still, where the original rotates the whole control triangle; the P slider, Reset button and board size are additions, and the speed runs from 0 to 20 at 50 ms a frame.

Press Play and count the six arcs. Then slide P between B and C and watch the status line change from constant width to a curve that bends inward.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
